items.headline: Army awards up to $2.2bn across five bases for microreactors
items.what_happened: The Army signed milestone-based Other Transaction Authority agreements worth up to $2.2 billion combined, running FY2027-FY2031, with five companies to build and operate microreactors: Antares at Fort Bragg, Radiant at Fort Benning, BWXT at Fort Campbell, General Atomics at Fort Hood, and Westinghouse Government Services at Fort Drum. Only Radiant disclosed its own award value, up to $750 million for 15 Kaleidos units; the Army declined to break out the other four. The five installations were narrowed down from a longer list of nine candidate sites that the Army and the Defense Innovation Unit identified in November 2025.
items.why_it_matters: This is the largest concentrated public bet on the microreactor class to date, and the Army's own program lead was candid that nobody knows what these reactors will actually cost and that some of the five vendors will likely fail before 2028 — the government is explicitly underwriting first-of-a-kind construction risk rather than waiting for a market price to form.
items.binding_note: Each vendor holds a signed, executed OTA agreement, not a preliminary selection — funds release against technical milestones for prototype construction and a first year of operation, after which the Army plans to shift to a power purchase agreement. Per-vendor dollar figures beyond Radiant's remain undisclosed.

items.headline: Antares to build three R1 microreactors at Fort Bragg
items.what_happened: The Army selected Antares Nuclear to own, build and operate a three-unit R1 deployment at Fort Bragg, home of the XVIII Airborne Corps, under Janus. Antares declined to disclose the contract's value but said its combined book across Janus, the Air Force ANPI award at Joint Base San Antonio, and Space Force work is now on the order of $1 billion. The R1 units, 100 kWe-1 MWe sodium heat-pipe reactors fueled by TRISO, build on the company's Mark-0 test reactor, which reached criticality at Idaho National Laboratory on June 4, 2026.
items.why_it_matters: Antares is now a three-program vendor (Janus, ANPI, Space Force) without a single disclosed contract value for any of them, so the $1 billion figure is entirely self-reported — a case study in how thin the public paper trail is even for a company winning federal reactor work.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement, not a mere selection; the dollar value of this specific award is undisclosed, only the combined cross-program total.

items.headline: Radiant wins largest Janus award, up to $750M for 15 units
items.what_happened: Radiant secured the largest of the five Janus awards, up to $750 million to develop and deploy 15 Kaleidos microreactors across Army installations by 2030, starting with a three-unit deployment at Fort Benning targeted for 2028. Radiant called it one of the largest contracts ever issued through the Defense Innovation Unit. The award adds to Radiant's existing Air Force ANPI selection at Buckley Space Force Base and its commercial Equinix agreement for 20 Kaleidos units.
items.why_it_matters: A single award now covers three quarters of the Janus program's disclosed dollar figure and 15 of its 20-plus planned units, meaning the program's near-term commercial track record will be dominated by one vendor and one reactor design.
items.binding_note: Radiant itself described this as a binding Janus agreement, the only one of the five vendors to publish its own award ceiling.

items.headline: BWXT to deploy 20 MWe BANR reactor at Fort Campbell
items.what_happened: BWXT Advanced Technologies will deploy a 20 MWe (75 MWth) configuration of its BANR high-temperature gas reactor at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, the largest single reactor in the Janus program. BWXT did not disclose the contract's value but confirmed a phased structure, with groundbreaking targeted for late 2028 and operation in the early 2030s. The design scales up BWXT's 1.5 MWe Project Pele microreactor, which delivered a full TRISO fuel core to the Department of Defense in late 2025.
items.why_it_matters: BWXT is the only Janus vendor that fabricates its own TRISO fuel, at its NRC-licensed Lynchburg, Virginia plant, which also supplies fuel to Antares and Radiant — making it a supplier to its own Janus competitors as well as a reactor vendor in its own right.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement; the specific dollar value was not disclosed.

items.headline: General Atomics to advance GA-TES microreactor at Fort Hood
items.what_happened: General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems will advance its GA-TES microreactor at Fort Hood, Texas through development, testing and site-planning milestones; the award's value was not disclosed. GA-TES is the only Janus reactor that does not use TRISO fuel — it runs on uranium-zirconium hydride drawing on General Atomics' TRIGA research-reactor heritage, is liquid-metal-cooled with natural circulation, and has a baseline output of about 5 MWe scalable to roughly 20 MWe. GA-EMS did not name a fuel supplier or utility partner for the site.
items.why_it_matters: GA-TES is the least mature of the five Janus designs by disclosed detail, and it is also the only one using a fuel form other than TRISO, so its supply chain and licensing path diverge from the rest of the program's four TRISO-based vendors.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement covering development and testing milestones, not yet a deployment commitment; the company is explicitly in a development phase.

items.headline: Westinghouse to bring eVinci to Fort Drum after Schumer push
items.what_happened: The Army selected Westinghouse Government Services to deploy its eVinci heat-pipe microreactor at Fort Drum, New York, home of the 10th Mountain Division; Westinghouse did not disclose output, schedule or contract value. POWER reported the selection followed a mid-August letter from Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to Army Secretary Dan Driscoll urging that Fort Drum be prioritized. Westinghouse is also the ANPI selectee at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana.
items.why_it_matters: This is a rare documented case of a named senator lobbying directly for a specific base's inclusion in a reactor siting decision, and it landed — worth watching whether other undisclosed sites got the same treatment without a public paper trail.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement, not a mere selection, though none of output, schedule or value has been disclosed for this specific pairing.

items.headline: Westinghouse eVinci reaches zero-power criticality in Nevada
items.what_happened: Westinghouse's eVinci microreactor design achieved zero-power criticality at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center, a National Nuclear Security Administration facility at the Nevada National Security Site, at 10:39 a.m. Pacific on August 24, 2026, two days before the Janus announcement named Westinghouse for Fort Drum. The test was completed in partnership with Los Alamos National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory.
items.why_it_matters: This is a genuine technical milestone, not a business announcement, and its timing two days ahead of a $2.2 billion Army award is a reminder that a company's demonstrated hardware progress and its federal contract wins are moving on separate, only loosely coordinated tracks.
items.binding_note: An achieved physical milestone (criticality), independently confirmed, not a company claim or a forward-looking target.

items.headline: Radiant locks in Standard Nuclear TRISO fabrication through 2031
items.what_happened: Radiant and Standard Nuclear announced a binding, multi-metric-ton TRISO fuel fabrication agreement extending through 2031. DOE-allocated HALEU will supply the enriched uranium; Standard Nuclear fabricates it into reactor-ready TRISO particle fuel for Kaleidos units under both the Janus and ANPI programs. Radiant said the agreement covers a distinct risk from HALEU access itself — the specialized fabrication capacity needed to turn allocated material into qualified fuel.
items.why_it_matters: Fuel fabrication capacity, not enrichment, is the supply-chain bottleneck this deal targets directly — a vendor can hold a HALEU allocation and still have nowhere to turn it into qualified fuel, and this agreement is Radiant buying its way out of that specific risk through the early 2030s.
items.binding_note: Described by Radiant as a binding, multi-metric-ton agreement with a fixed end date, not an MOU or exploratory arrangement.

items.headline: Antares signs Standard Nuclear TRISO deal, options more through 2035
items.what_happened: Antares announced a binding agreement under which Standard Nuclear will supply 1 metric ton of TRISO fuel, with Antares holding an option for up to seven additional metric tons through 2035. Antares had previously said it expected to source TRISO from both Standard Nuclear and BWXT, but has not disclosed a binding agreement with BWXT. The company has not said how much of the Standard Nuclear fuel will support Janus, ANPI, or its Space Force work.
items.why_it_matters: Coming one day after the Janus awards and one week after Radiant's own Standard Nuclear deal, this shows fuel fabrication capacity is becoming a real point of competition between microreactor vendors, not just a shared industry dependency.
items.binding_note: The initial 1 metric ton supply is a binding agreement; the additional seven metric tons are an option, not a commitment.
